evidence_set: Methadone, overdose, 11 cohorts: pooled 2.6 (2.1 to 3.3) overdose deaths per 1,000 person-years in treatment and 12.7 (6.9 to 23.4) out; unadjusted rate difference 10.0 (2.6 to 17.4) and rate ratio 4.80 (2.90 to 7.96); heterogeneity I² 66% in treatment and 97% out. Buprenorphine (one cohort): 1.4 in and 4.6 out. Editors' reading of Fig 3: the overdose rate was higher out of treatment in each of the 11 methadone cohorts, though in Buster 2002 only barely (2.2 in, 2.4 out), and Table 4 gives that cohort's own unadjusted out-to-in overdose ratio as 0.87.
Results › Overdose mortality during and after opioid substitution treatment, 1st paragraph (p. 4); Fig 3 (p. 10); Table 4, Buster 2002 row (p. 9)

Trend analysis (P = 0.04 for departure from linearity): the pooled all-cause rate fell from 37.4 to 6.4 per 1,000 person-years over the first four weeks of methadone treatment and was fairly stable after; after leaving it stayed between 24.1 and 35.2 during the first two weeks out and then declined. In Fig 4 the first-period rate in treatment was 37.5 in Degenhardt 2009 (first two weeks) against 15.1, 7.7, 9.6 and 4.4 in the other four cohorts (first four weeks). Editors' reading of Figs 4 and 5: in Fig 5 the only cohort rate plotted before one week of treatment is Degenhardt 2009's, and the other cohorts' earliest plotted rates are lower, so the steep early fall rests largely on one cohort.

Five methadone cohorts and one buprenorphine cohort reported all-cause out-to-in rate ratios adjusted to various degrees for demographics, severity of drug use, treatment delivery and comorbidity (Degenhardt 2009 only for age, sex and calendar year): after adjustment the ratios were unchanged in two methadone cohorts (Degenhardt 2009, 1.91 to 1.88; Nosyk 2015, 3.04 to 2.94), 15.5% to 35.5% larger in three, and 16.8% larger in the buprenorphine cohort; overdose ratios were unchanged in three methadone cohorts and 25.8% and 28.6% larger in two, Evans 2015 and Nosyk 2015, whose overdose ratios combine maintenance with detoxification (Evans) or include never-treated participants (Nosyk, 73.3% of person-years out of treatment) (Table 4 footnote). The authors describe the adjustment factors as measured mostly at baseline.

Results › All cause mortality during and after opioid substitution treatment, 4th paragraph, and Overdose mortality during and after opioid substitution treatment, 2nd paragraph (p. 4); Table 4 and footnotes (p. 9); Discussion › Strengths and limitations, 2nd paragraph (p. 12)

The authors note that methadone's long half-life could contribute to the rise in deaths in the first three to four days after leaving, but that deaths rose markedly across the whole first four weeks compared with the treatment period; they suggest this could be explained by loss of tolerance to the toxic effects of heroin, assuming that many people return to use, and probably by use of several legal and illicit substances; they note similar peaks after prison release or hospital discharge, where tolerance is probably diminished, and that deaths from suicide and injury are also more common in that period. The review had no data on tolerance or drug use after leaving.

Limitations stated by the authors: the same people are compared in and out of treatment, but they leave and re-enter treatment non-randomly, so there could still be a large potential for confounding in crude comparisons, and confounders would need measuring at each exit and re-entry; dropouts are more likely among people at higher risk of death while out of treatment (informative censoring); the amount and direction of the resulting bias in the pooled estimates is hard to assess with the available information; studies were from high-income countries; overdose deaths when substitution medicines were obtained on illicit markets were not captured; a delayed record of leaving could misclassify deaths out of treatment as in treatment (making the estimates conservative); inconsistent overdose definitions and cause-of-death coding could misclassify deaths, which would tend to undercount overdose deaths.

evidence_set: The editorial says that death is an uncommon but catastrophic outcome of opioid withdrawal and that complications of withdrawal are often underestimated and monitored inadequately; it calls the withdrawal syndrome well delineated (citing DSM-5, listed as the 2013 DSM) and then, without a citation, says it is generally characterised as a flu-like illness, subjectively severe but objectively mild, in contrast with the life-threatening alcohol and benzodiazepine withdrawal syndromes.

evidence_set: Over 20 months, 137 consecutive people dependent on opiates who were receiving detoxification as part of a 28-day inpatient treatment programme, and who consented to follow-up, were recruited; 5 died within 12 months of discharge, 3 of them after a drug overdose within the first four months; 103 were interviewed at a mean of 8.7 months after discharge, and a records search showed the other 29 alive one year after discharge, so all 137 are accounted for (5 + 103 + 29, editors' count). How deaths were ascertained, and how survival to one year was checked for those interviewed, is not described.

To test whether loss of tolerance raised the risk of overdose, the authors grouped people by their presumed opiate tolerance on leaving treatment: 43 'still tolerant' who failed to complete detoxification; 57 'reduced tolerance' who completed the prescribed detoxification but left the programme early; 37 'lost tolerance' who completed detoxification and the whole inpatient programme. The three overdose deaths, all within four months of leaving, were all in the last group; the two deaths not related to overdose, both in people who had relapsed, were one in the 'lost tolerance' group (end-stage renal failure) and one in the 'reduced tolerance' group (Clostridium welchii infection); nobody in the 'still tolerant' group died (Fisher's exact test, df = 2, P = 0.02, without saying whether all deaths or overdose deaths were compared). Mean time to the follow-up interview was 9.5, 8.7 and 7.8 months in the three groups. Editors' calculation (exact binomial 95% intervals): overdose deaths 3 of 37 (8.1%, 1.7% to 21.9%) against 0 of 100 in the two other groups together (0% to 3.6%). No measure of tolerance is reported; drug use after discharge is reported only as relapse in the two people whose deaths were not due to overdose.
